passage:
Keerthana, you asked why I stuck that note on the office printer: REAL POLICE DON'T ARREST ON VIDEO. Sit. Your Ojas Sir will tell you.
Eight years ago, when I was twenty-five and new to this city, a man called saying he was a customs officer. A parcel in my name, full of fake passports. He switched to video. Uniform, office, flag. He said I was under arrest and must stay on the call and tell no one.
My heart was pounding. But my father had told me one thing: when someone rushes you and says tell no one, that is exactly when you tell someone.
So I said, "I'll call your office myself," and hung up. He called back six times. I didn't answer.
I found the customs helpline on the official website. No such case. Then I called my father, and then the cybercrime helpline, and reported the number.
That's the whole trick. Hang up. Verify. Tell.

qa.q: What did the caller claim was in the parcel?
qa.a: He claimed the parcel was full of fake passports.

qa.q: How did young Ojas feel during the video call?
qa.a: His heart was pounding with fear, yet he held on to his father's advice about rushing and secrecy.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story broke the scam?
qa.a: Saying he would call the office himself and hanging up, then checking the official customs helpline, showed there was no case.

qa.q: How did the caller react to being hung up on?
qa.a: The caller rang back six times, showing that the pressure was a tactic to stop Ojas from checking with anyone.

grounding: Ojas recalls hanging up on a fake customs officer, calling the official helpline himself, telling his father and reporting the number.

passage:
Madhav was on the last metro home, phone at six percent, when the video call came. A man in a courtroom-style office said a warrant had been issued in his name. "Stay on camera. Don't disconnect. Tell anyone and the warrant covers them too."
Madhav's pulse jumped. Then he noticed what they were asking for: secrecy, speed, and soon, surely, money.
"I'll verify this with the police station myself," he said, and ended the call. It rang again at once. He declined it and switched to airplane mode to save battery.
At his stop he plugged the phone into a café socket, found his local police station's number on the official website, and called. The duty officer sighed. "No warrants are served on video calls, sir. Report the number."
He called his brother Vaibhav next, then reported the number to the cybercrime helpline. Four percent left. Enough.

qa.q: What was Madhav's phone battery at when the call came?
qa.a: His phone was at six percent.

qa.q: What did Madhav realise after his pulse jumped?
qa.a: He realised they wanted secrecy, speed and soon money, which made him suspicious rather than only afraid.

qa.q: Which of Madhav's steps worked, and why?
qa.a: Hanging up, calling the police station on the number from the official website, telling Vaibhav and reporting to the cybercrime helpline broke the secrecy and confirmed the call was fake.

qa.q: How did the duty officer see the call?
qa.a: The duty officer saw it as a familiar scam, sighing because no warrants are served on video calls.

grounding: A young man on a late metro hangs up on a fake court call, verifies with the police himself, tells his brother and reports the number.

passage:
Kishore was at his desk in the Pune office when his phone rang. "This is Delhi Police. A SIM in your name is linked to a fraud case. Stay on the line. An officer will video call you. Do not inform anyone."
Kishore felt a jolt of fear. Then he remembered his brother Nilesh's warning last month: no real agency arrests anyone on a video call, and none ever asks for money to clear your name.
He said, "I'll call the police station myself," and hung up.
His heart was still racing. He looked up the official number of his local police station on the government website and called. The officer laughed tiredly. "We get ten of these complaints a day, sir. It's fake."
Kishore called Nilesh. "You were right. They tried it on me."
"Did you pay anything?"
"Nothing."
"Good. Now report the number on the cybercrime helpline." Kishore did it before lunch.

qa.q: Who did the caller claim to be?
qa.a: Delhi Police.

qa.q: How did Kishore feel when the caller said he was linked to a fraud case?
qa.a: Kishore felt a jolt of fear, his heart racing, before remembering his brother's warning.

qa.q: What steps did Kishore take after hanging up?
qa.a: He called his local police station on the official number from the government website, told Nilesh, and reported the number to the cybercrime helpline.

qa.q: How did the local police officer react to Kishore's call?
qa.a: The officer seemed tired and unsurprised, saying they get many such complaints a day and it was fake.

grounding: It shows an adult hanging up on a fake police call, calling the official number himself, telling family and reporting it.

passage:
"Customs department? A parcel in my name?" Lakshmi put the phone on speaker so her sister Tanuja could hear.
"Yes, madam. Drugs and passports were found. You must stay on video call with our officer. Do not tell family."
Tanuja shook her head hard and mouthed, "Hang up."
"Can I call you back on your official number?" Lakshmi asked.
"No! If you disconnect, a warrant will be issued immediately."
Lakshmi's hand was shaking. Tanuja took the phone gently and ended the call.
"Tanuja! What if it's real?"
"Real customs don't arrest you on video, and they don't pay you a phone visit to ask for money. Let's check." Tanuja searched the courier company's official website and called their helpline. No parcel in Lakshmi's name.
Lakshmi sat down, breathing out. "They sounded so official."
"That's their job. Now let's report this number to the cybercrime helpline, and tell Amma so she knows too."

qa.q: What did the caller say was found in the parcel?
qa.a: Drugs and passports.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi feel during the call?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt frightened, her hand shaking, and afraid a warrant would be issued if she hung up.

qa.q: What steps did Lakshmi and Tanuja take?
qa.a: They ended the call, checked with the courier company's official helpline, reported the number to the cybercrime helpline, and planned to tell Amma.

qa.q: How did Tanuja see the call?
qa.a: Tanuja saw it as a scam from the start, knowing real customs don't arrest people on video or demand money.

grounding: It shows an adult hanging up on a fake customs call, verifying through the official number, telling family and reporting it.

passage:
I'm Yusuf, and last month I nearly got "digitally arrested."
The call came at eleven in the morning. A man said he was from customs. A parcel from Thailand in my name, with fake passports. He transferred me to a "police officer" on video. Uniform, flag, badge. "You are a suspect. Do not tell your wife or anyone. Transfer your savings for verification."
My knees went weak. For a minute I believed him.
Then I remembered a line from a news article: real agencies don't arrest people over video or ask for money to clear your name.
I said, "I will call the customs office myself," and hung up. He called back six times. I didn't answer.
I found the official customs helpline on the government website and called. No such case. Then I called my wife, Nirmala, at her office. She said, "Come home. Let's report it together." We filed a complaint on the cybercrime helpline that evening.

qa.q: Where did the parcel supposedly come from?
qa.a: From Thailand.

qa.q: How did Yusuf feel when the "officer" appeared on video?
qa.a: Yusuf felt frightened, with weak knees, and for a minute believed the caller.

qa.q: What steps did Yusuf take after hanging up?
qa.a: Yusuf called the official customs helpline from the government website, told Nirmala, and reported it to the cybercrime helpline that evening.

qa.q: How did Nirmala respond when Yusuf called?
qa.a: Nirmala was calm and supportive, telling Yusuf to come home so they could report it together.

grounding: An adult recalls hanging up on a fake customs and police call, verifying through the official number, telling family and reporting it.

passage:
Supervisor's note, call-centre floor, Tuesday.
At 11:20 Francis's mobile rang at his desk. I saw him go stiff. Afterwards he told me the caller said he was from the "Cyber Crime Branch", that a SIM in his name was linked to a money-laundering case, and that he would be put on a video call and must not disconnect or tell anyone.
Francis did not argue. He said, "I'll call the police station myself," and hung up. His hands were shaking. He looked up the local police station's official number on the government website, not the one the caller gave, and they confirmed they make no arrests over video and ask for no payments. He then phoned his sister, and together we reported it on the cybercrime helpline before lunch.
I've asked Francis to walk the team through it at Friday's meeting. He agreed, looking relieved.
Varun

qa.q: What did the caller say a SIM in Francis's name was linked to?
qa.a: A money-laundering case.

qa.q: How was Francis feeling after he hung up?
qa.a: Francis was frightened, his hands shaking, but steady enough to check; later he looked relieved.

qa.q: Which of Francis's steps made the difference?
qa.a: Hanging up, finding the police station's number himself on the government website, telling his sister, and reporting it to the cybercrime helpline.

qa.q: How might Francis's teammates benefit on Friday?
qa.a: They will hear exactly what such a call sounds like and what to do, so they may feel less frightened and more prepared if it happens to them.

grounding: Shows a person who hangs up on a fake agency, calls the official number himself, tells family and reports to the cybercrime helpline.
